title: Onion Bhaji
subtitle: Crispy spiced onion fritters in a chickpea flour batter
excerpt: Thin-sliced onion mixed into a spiced chickpea flour batter with cumin, coriander, and green chilli, then fried until crisp and golden. The classic curry-house starter that is also a good street food snack.
sourceNotes: Bhaji (pakora in north India and Pakistan) is a deep-fried fritter made from vegetables dipped in a spiced chickpea flour batter. Onion bhaji became the standard curry-house starter in Britain. The British version typically uses a thick, binding batter rather than a light dipping batter. Madhur Jaffrey, Madhur Jaffrey's Indian Cookery (BBC Books, 1982) covers pakora technique.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The batter can rest for up to 30 minutes before frying. Resting lets the flour hydrate and the bhajis fry more evenly.

glossaryTerms.definition: Also called gram flour or besan, this is dried chickpeas ground into a fine powder. It forms the basis of bhaji batter, pakoras, and many South Asian flatbreads. It has a slightly nutty flavour and fries to a crisp, stable crust.

content.text: Onion bhajis are thin-sliced onion in a thick

batter spiced with cumin, coriander, and green chilli, fried at 170°C. The batter is thick enough to bind the onion into a fritter rather than a thin coating, which gives bhajis their characteristic layered texture. The rest time after mixing allows the flour to hydrate so the fritters hold together.
The onion releases liquid as it sits. Mix everything together and leave for 10 minutes; the batter will tighten up as the onion releases moisture into the flour. You should not need to add water.

Combine the {{onion}} of sliced onion with {{chickpea-flour}} of chickpea flour, cumin seeds, ground coriander, turmeric, green chilli, fresh coriander, and salt in a large bowl. Mix thoroughly with your hands, squeezing the onion into the flour. Leave to rest for 10 minutes. The onion will release liquid and the batter will tighten. If the mixture seems dry after resting, add water one teaspoon at a time. It should hold together when you press a small amount into a ball.
Heat the oil in a large saucepan to 170°C. Test with a small drop of batter: it should sizzle and float immediately.

Scoop rough tablespoons of the mixture and lower gently into the oil. Do not flatten them: irregular shapes fry more evenly than neat balls. Fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until golden and crisp. Fry in batches of 4 to 5 to avoid crowding.
Drain on kitchen paper and season with salt. Serve immediately with chutney or raita.

rows.symptom: Bhajis fall apart in the oil
rows.cause: Batter too dry, or not enough rest time for the onion to release liquid
rows.fix: Leave the batter for a full 10 minutes after mixing. If it still crumbles, add 1 teaspoon of water and mix again.
Check the oil is at 170°C before frying. Low-temperature bhajis absorb oil rather than crisping quickly.

rows.cause: Bhajis too thick, or oil too hot so outside cooked faster than inside
rows.fix: Keep bhajis small and irregular. Fry at 170°C rather than higher; this gives the heat time to penetrate the centre.

content.text: Onion bhaji became the standard curry-house starter in Britain from the 1970s. It arrives before the main course with mango chutney and mint sauce. The dish comes from the pakora fritter tradition of north India and Pakistan. The British restaurant version uses onion as the standard filling and a firmer batter than the lighter original.
